title: "Send a doctor now"
stem:
You are an F2 doctor in an out-of-hours GP service. You call back Mrs Hart, whose daughter, 8, has a temperature of 38°C and a sore throat. The child is eating, drinking and playing.

When you explain that a home visit isn't needed, and offer an appointment at the base, Mrs Hart becomes abusive, swearing at you and demanding that a doctor visits.
instruction: Choose the 3 most appropriate actions to take in this situation.

options.text: Arrange the visit to end the call.
options.brief: Uses a limited resource to avoid conflict.
options.detailed: This would end the confrontation, but visits are limited and may be needed for sicker patients.

options.text: End the call immediately because of her abuse.
options.detailed: You don't have to tolerate abuse, and services allow calls to be ended after a warning. But ending it immediately, without safety-netting, leaves her daughter's care unresolved.

options.text: Tell her she will be reported to the police for her abuse.
options.detailed: Abuse can sometimes be reported, but threatening it now is likely to make things worse.

options.text: Stay calm, and acknowledge that she is worried about her daughter.
options.detailed: Her anger may come from worry. Acknowledging it, calmly, may help her listen.

options.text: Ask a few more questions to check that your assessment is right.
options.brief: Her strength of feeling is a reason to double-check.
options.detailed: Parents often notice things that are hard to describe. Checking again, for example about breathing, rash or drowsiness, makes sure you haven't missed anything.

options.text: Tell her to take her daughter to the Emergency Department instead.
options.brief: Not clinically needed, and adds pressure on ED.
options.detailed: The base appointment is more appropriate for her daughter's symptoms.

options.text: Pass the call to another doctor.
options.brief: May be needed later, but doesn't help now.
options.detailed: Another clinician may help if the conversation breaks down, but trying to resolve it yourself first is better.

options.text: Explain the options and when to call back or call 999.
options.detailed: Offering the base appointment again, and explaining which signs mean she should call back or call 999, keeps her daughter safe whatever she decides.

explanation.issue: This tests how you handle an abusive caller while keeping a child safe and using resources fairly.
explanation.keyDetails: The child seems well. The mother is worried and angry. A base appointment is available.
explanation.reasoning: [D] de-escalates, [E] double-checks, and [H] safety-nets. The distractors give in ([A]), end the call unsafely ([B]), escalate ([C]), misdirect ([F]), or pass it on ([G]).
explanation.competing: [B] is the hard distractor: you can end an abusive call, but not before her daughter's care is safe.

references.title: Good medical practice
references.note: Domain 2, communicating with patients and families; Domain 1, providing safe care.
